\section[\hi{पानी} \hi{रोटी}]{\hi{पानी}, \hi{रोटी} (pānī, roṭī) — water (the "drinkable thing") and bread}

\label{lesson:HI-C15-paani-roti}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Hindi's everyday word for water isn't the ancient Sanskrit word you might expect — it names water by what you \textbf{do} with it, not by what it \textbf{is}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{पानी} — "the drinkable thing"}
\textbf{\hi{पानी}} (\emph{pānī}) = "\textbf{water}." Sanskrit actually has older, more "basic" words for water — \textbf{\hi{आप्}} (\emph{āp}) and \textbf{\hi{जल}} (\emph{jala}) among them — but Hindi's everyday word descends from neither. It comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{पानीय}} (\emph{pānīya}), built on the verb \textbf{\hi{पा}} (\emph{pā}), "\textbf{to drink}," plus a suffix meaning roughly "\textbf{fit for}." So \emph{pānīya}, and Hindi's \emph{pānī} after it, literally means "\textbf{the drinkable thing}" — water defined by its use, not named as a substance in its own right.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{रोटी} — bread, honestly uncertain in origin}
\textbf{\hi{रोटी}} (\emph{roṭī}) = "\textbf{bread, flatbread}" — the everyday word for the flatbreads (roti, chapati-style breads) central to North Indian meals. Be honest: unlike \emph{pānī}, \emph{roṭī}'s deeper history is \textbf{not cleanly traced} back through Sanskrit the way many everyday Hindi words are. It comes through Prakrit \textbf{\hi{रोट्ट}} (\emph{roṭṭa}, "a kind of bread") from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{रोटिका}} (\emph{roṭikā}); beyond that, one proposal (Turner's Indo-Aryan dictionary) tentatively links it to a root meaning "\textbf{to strike / to press or crush}" — perhaps evoking the pounding and flattening of dough — but this is genuinely uncertain, one guess among scholars rather than a settled chain. Worth knowing honestly rather than forcing a confident derivation that isn't there.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "pānī" — water, "the drinkable thing"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the root — "pā," to drink, + "-nīya," fit for{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "roṭī" — bread, flatbread{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Does \textbf{\hi{पानी}} come from Sanskrit's ancient water-words, \emph{āp} or \emph{jala}? (\textbf{No} — from \textbf{\hi{पानीय}} \emph{pānīya}, "the drinkable thing," from \textbf{\hi{पा}} \emph{pā}, "to drink.") Is \textbf{\hi{रोटी}}'s etymology as clearly traced as \emph{pānī}'s? (\textbf{No} — it traces to Prakrit \emph{roṭṭa} < Sanskrit \emph{roṭikā}, but beyond that the deeper root is genuinely uncertain — one proposal links it to "striking/pressing" dough, not a settled chain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
